text: Probabilities aren't fixed facts about the world — they depend on what you already know. The chance a random customer churns is one number; the chance a customer on the free plan churns may be very different. Conditional probability updates a probability given information, and independence is the special case where information changes nothing. Every classifier, from logistic regression to a random forest, is estimating a conditional probability.

Take 1,000 illustrative customers split evenly between free and paid plans. Overall churn is 200 of 1,000, so P of churn is 0.2. But look inside each plan: among free customers, 150 of 500 churned, so P of churn given Free is 0.3. Among paid customers it's only 0.1. Knowing the plan changed the probability from 0.2 to 0.3 or 0.1.

The conditional probability of A given B is P of A and B, divided by P of B. In words: restrict attention to cases where B happened, then ask what fraction of those also had A. Checking the table: P of Free and churn is 0.15, P of Free is 0.5, so P of churn given Free is 0.15 over 0.5, equals 0.3 — it matches. In pandas, conditioning is just filtering and then taking a mean, exactly what groupby already does.

Rearranging the definition gives the multiplication rule: P of A and B equals P of B times P of A given B. That's how we compute both happening. Drawing two cards without replacement, the probability both are aces is 4 over 52 times 3 over 51, about 0.0045 — the second factor is conditional, since once one ace is gone only 3 of the remaining 51 cards are aces. Squaring 4 over 52 would be wrong, because it ignores that the first draw changed the deck.

Events A and B are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other — P of A given B equals P of A — and the multiplication rule simplifies to P of A and B equals P of A times P of B. Our plan and churn are clearly not independent, since 0.3 doesn't equal 0.2. Two dice, though, should be independent.

Checking with a million simulated dice rolls: A is first die equals 6, B is second die 4 or more. A's probability is 0.1665, B's is 0.5003, and A-and-B is 0.0831 — almost exactly matching A times B, 0.0833. That near-match is the signature of independence. With real data the numbers will never match exactly, so Chapter 5 covers a formal test.

Three traps to avoid. First, reversing the condition: P of churn given Free is 0.3, but P of Free given churn is 150 over 200, 0.75 — different questions, different answers, and Bayes' theorem next lesson shows how to convert between them. Second, independent is not the same as mutually exclusive — mutually exclusive events can't both happen, which actually makes them dependent.

Third, don't assume independence just because it's convenient. Many models assume independent observations, but customers in the same household, sessions from the same user, and measurements over time are often correlated — assuming independence when it's false can make results look more certain than they are. To recap: P of A given B is P of A and B over P of B, the multiplication rule chains conditionals, and independence is when conditioning changes nothing. Next: Bayes' theorem.
